verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.29–30 (Gita Press / Shankara numbering; Sastri prints it as '28-29' and '30'). Vedabase (Prabhupada) splits these lines differently: they sit in its 1.28b–1.30a. Vireswarananda's Sridhara edition prints them as 1.29–1.30a.
attribution_note: Arjuna speaking to Krishna is right. Small point: the setting says he 'collapses' here; at this verse he is describing his body failing. He actually sits down and drops the bow at 1.47.
translation_note: Our Sanskrit and ref cover 1.29 and 1.30, but the English renders only 1.29 (limbs, mouth, trembling, hair). It leaves out 1.30: the Gandiva bow slipping from his hand, his skin burning, being unable to stand, and his mind seeming to spin. Add the second half or narrow the ref and Sanskrit to 1.29. The line's 'racing body' and 'panic attack' are modern framing; the verse itself names trembling, not a racing heart.
context: Krishna has driven the chariot between the two armies at Arjuna's request. Arjuna sees teachers, uncles, sons, grandsons and friends on both sides and is overcome by pity. Here he describes what that sight is doing to his body. Next he says he sees bad omens and wants no victory, kingdom or pleasure bought by killing his own people.

key_terms.sense: my limbs sink / give way
and my mouth dries up completely
trembling of the body … hair standing on end
the Gandiva bow slips from my hand (1.30)
and my mind seems to whirl (1.30)

core_teaching: This verse isn't a teaching. It is Arjuna's honest report of grief and fear taking over his body. The classical commentators treat the whole stretch from 1.2 to 2.9 as the diagnosis: grief and confusion that come from the sense of 'mine'. The rest of the Gita answers it.

commentaries.gist: Shankara does not comment on chapter 1 verse by verse. At 2.10 he says 1.2–2.9 shows where grief and delusion come from: the feeling 'I am theirs and they are mine', which overpowers clear judgement.

Closing chapter 1, Ramanuja calls Arjuna noble and compassionate, affectionate even towards kin who had tried to kill him. Overcome by pity and fear of doing wrong, he shrank back, grieving at losing them.

commentaries.who: A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada (modern, ISKCON)
commentaries.gist: Trembling and hair standing on end can come either from spiritual ecstasy or from ordinary fear. Here they are fear, ultimately of loss of life, and they show a body-centred view of oneself.

practical_reading: It works as a way to name the body's signs of overwhelm (shaking, dry mouth, a spinning mind) before trying to fix anything. The Gita takes the breakdown seriously enough to give it a full chapter before any advice begins.
misreadings: Not simply cowardice. Ramanuja reads pity, love for kin and fear of doing wrong; Shankara reads grief and confusion born of attachment.
Not a clinical description. Calling it a 'panic attack' is a modern analogy, so present it as one.
Not a verse that tells the reader to push through bodily distress. It only describes the distress.
cautions: The setting is a battle against one's own family; killing kin is what Arjuna dreads.
Prabhupada's reading (fear from a bodily view of life) can sound dismissive to someone with real anxiety symptoms. Use it lightly.
Used on Day 1 of 'work feels unsafe'. Later Gita verses push Arjuna to stand up and fight; the writer should not carry that over as 'stay and endure an unsafe workplace'.
speaks_to: body-level dread before a confrontation or hard conversation
freezing when people you care about are on the other side
feeling that you are falling apart before something you have to do
not_for: someone having physical symptoms that may need medical help; the verse names distress but cannot treat it
a reader being harmed at work, if the plan goes on to frame staying as duty
research_note: Sridhara only glosses the words for this verse (trembling, hair bristling, bow slipping, skin scorched), so it is not listed as a separate commentary. Sivananda gives only a translation here. The Prabhupada gist comes from the Vedabase page for its 1.29 (vepathuś ca …).

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.47 in the Gita Press / Shankara text (also Ramanuja tr. Govindacharya, Sridhara tr. Vireswarananda, Sivananda). Vedabase (Prabhupada) numbers it 1.46 because its chapter 1 has 46 verses.
attribution_note: Sanjaya to Dhritarashtra is right. Ramanuja's note explicitly frames it as Sanjaya telling Dhritarashtra.
context: This verse closes chapter 1. Arjuna has argued that killing kin would destroy families and their ways of life, and has said he would rather be killed unarmed. Sanjaya, narrating to the blind king, reports that Arjuna drops his bow and arrows and sits down in the chariot. Chapter 2 opens with Krishna rebuking this weakness.

key_terms.sense: he sat down on the seat (floor) of the chariot
casting aside the bow along with its arrows
his mind shaken / agitated by grief
in the battle, i.e. in the middle of the battlefield

core_teaching: The narrative low point: grief has taken away Arjuna's will to act. The commentators read it as the state the teaching is about to address, not as a final verdict on him.

commentaries.gist: Arjuna was compassionate towards kin who had plotted to burn him alive. Overcome by pity and fear of unrighteousness, he refused to fight. Grieving at the thought of separation from them, he let the bow go and sat down.
Sridhara treats it as Sanjaya answering 'what happened next?'. Arjuna, his mind agitated by grief, sat down on the chariot in the midst of battle.
At 2.10 Shankara says that once grief and delusion overpower discrimination, people abandon their own duties. Arjuna withdrawing from his duty as a warrior is his example.

practical_reading: It names the moment of putting everything down when you can't go on. The story doesn't end there: the next verses are about getting help and finding a way forward.
misreadings: Not the Gita's verdict that giving up is right or wrong. It is the starting point the teaching answers.
Not a call to shame someone for stopping. Ramanuja stresses Arjuna's compassion.
cautions: Used on Day 1 of 'losing hope': it mirrors the low point. The writer should point forward (2.7, where he asks for help) and not leave the reader at the collapse.
Shankara's frame calls this grief 'delusion'. Do not tell a hopeless reader that their despair is a delusion.
The battle context (killing kin) sits right behind the verse.
speaks_to: the moment you put everything down and sit with it
feeling too overwhelmed by grief to go on
being stuck between duty and love
not_for: a reader who needs to be told they are not failing, if the reading frames stopping as weakness
research_note: Sivananda gives only a translation for this verse, with no commentary.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.7 (same in all editions checked: Sastri/Shankara, Govindacharya/Ramanuja, Vireswarananda/Sridhara, Sivananda).
attribution_note: The speaker and listener fields (Arjuna to Krishna) are right, but the setting sentence reads 'Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed…'. This verse is Arjuna's plea to Krishna. Fix the setting to something like 'Arjuna, in tears and refusing to fight, asks Krishna to teach him.'
translation_note: Acceptable. 'Weakness' for kārpaṇya-doṣa is one reading; Sastri has 'helplessness', Sivananda 'pity', and Sridhara 'helplessness and sin'. 'I have come to you' understates prapannam ('who has taken refuge in / surrendered to you'); consider 'I take refuge in you'.
context: Krishna has just told Arjuna to shake off his faint-heartedness and stand up (2.2–3). Arjuna replies that he cannot fight his revered elders Bhishma and Drona, and does not know which outcome would be worse (2.4–6). Here he gives up arguing and asks to be taught. Two verses later he says 'I will not fight' and falls silent, and Krishna begins teaching at 2.11.

key_terms.sense: my natural disposition struck down by the fault of helplessness / pity
my mind bewildered about what is right (dharma)
what is decisively (certainly) the better / highest good
I am your disciple … one who has taken refuge in you

core_teaching: Arjuna admits that his own judgement has failed him and asks, as a student, for a clear answer. Commentators see this surrender of pride as what makes the teaching possible.

commentaries.gist: Two things overcame his natural courage: helplessness at the thought of living on after killing them, and fear of the sin of destroying family. Unsure whether a warrior may quit battle to beg, he asks as a disciple taking refuge.

Arjuna humbly approaches Krishna as disciple and refuge-seeker. Krishna sees him undone by misplaced affection and pity, mistaking a lawful war for wrong, and resolves to teach self-knowledge joined to action done without interest in results.

Shankara reads 1.2–2.9 as showing how grief and delusion, born of 'mine'-ness, overpower judgement and make people abandon their duty. Because only self-knowledge removes them, Krishna begins teaching at 2.11.

practical_reading: Clarity often starts with admitting 'I don't know what's right here' and asking someone wiser, humbly and with a real question, rather than arguing for the choice you have already half made.
misreadings: Not a model of handing your judgement over completely. The rest of the Gita reasons with Arjuna at length.
Not proof that compassion is a defect. The commentators fault the confusion that pity caused here, not kindness itself.
cautions: Some renderings call Arjuna's pity a 'taint' (Sivananda). A reader whose distress comes from caring about people should not come away feeling their care is a flaw.
speaks_to: being torn between two choices that both seem wrong
admitting you are confused and need guidance
the first honest step of asking for help
not_for: someone being pressured to defer to an authority figure against their own conscience
research_note: Shankara has no separate bhashya on 2.7; his comment is the introduction at 2.10, which covers 1.2–2.9. Sivananda gives only a translation here.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.13 (same in all editions checked).
translation_note: The translation is faithful. The line ('The wise aren't thrown by the next change') blurs the verse's real subject, which is death and passing into another body, not just ageing. That may be a deliberate softening for a grief plan, but the writer should know the verse is about death.
context: Krishna has just smiled at Arjuna's grief and told him the wise mourn neither those who have died nor those still alive (2.11), since none of them ever did not exist (2.12). This verse is his first illustration. Next he turns to pleasure and pain as passing sense-contacts that must be endured (2.14–15).

key_terms.sense: the embodied one, the self that lives in the body
childhood, youth, old age
the attaining of another body (at death)
the steady / wise person is not deluded or thrown into confusion

core_teaching: The self stays the same through childhood, youth and old age, and it passes into another body in the same way. Death is therefore one more transition of the body, and the wise are not bewildered by it.

commentaries.gist: The Self passes unchanged through the stages of life. It does not die when childhood ends or get born when youth begins. It enters another body just as unchanged, so the wise are not troubled.
Nobody grieves moving from infancy to youth, so the wise do not grieve moving between bodies. Selves are eternal, bound by past deeds, and win freedom by doing their duties without craving the fruit.

Answering the objection that individual souls are born and die: across life's stages we know 'I am the same person', and the self takes a new body through the subtle body. A newborn's instinct to suckle shows past impressions.

practical_reading: Teachers use the familiar sense of being the same 'me' who was once a child to make a continuing self feel intuitive. The steadiness it offers is not being thrown when the body changes.
misreadings: Not a claim that ageing or death doesn't matter. It is about not being thrown into confusion by them.
Not just about ageing. The second half is about death and rebirth.
cautions: This passage teaches rebirth. To a newly bereaved reader, a doctrine that the dead simply move on can feel like it skips over their loss.
In context the verse supports Krishna's argument that the wise do not grieve (2.11). Writers should not pass that on as 'you should not grieve'.
speaks_to: noticing how much you have changed and are still you
wanting a sense of continuity beyond a loss
not_for: someone in the first raw days of a bereavement who needs their grief acknowledged, not explained
readers who do not hold a belief in rebirth, unless it is framed as the Gita's view
research_note: Sivananda's note closely matches Shankara's (no break in the self through death), so it is not listed separately.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.14 (same in all editions checked).
context: Just after the image of the self passing through childhood, youth and old age (2.13), Krishna anticipates a further worry: even if the self is eternal, we still suffer heat and cold, pleasure and pain. He says these come and go and must be borne. The next verse (2.15) says the steady person who is not shaken by them is fit for immortality.

key_terms.sense: contacts of the senses with their objects
givers of cold and heat, pleasure and pain
they arrive and depart; they are impermanent
endure them, bear them patiently

core_teaching: Pleasure and pain arise when the senses meet things, and by nature they begin and end. So bear them without being carried away by either joy or grief.

commentaries.gist: Cold or heat that pleases at one moment hurts at another. Because sense-contacts begin and end, they are impermanent, so endure them bravely and do not hand yourself over to joy or grief because of them.
Cold and heat stand for every kind of experience. Bear them with courage until your appointed duty is complete. They come and go, and they cannot disturb one whose karma has run out.

Arjuna might say he grieves his own pain at losing them. Meeting or parting from what we love brings pleasure and pain, as rain and sun bring cold and heat. Being transient, they should be borne without elation or despondency.
The same object pleases at one moment and hurts at another, so sensations are impermanent. It is the mind that feels pleasure and pain. Bear them patiently and cultivate a balanced mind.

practical_reading: In stress, the verse invites you to notice that this discomfort, like weather, has a beginning and an end. Patience means bearing it without adding panic or despair.
misreadings: Not a call to tolerate harm, abuse or unsafe conditions. Those are not passing sensations to wait out (as our misuse note says).
Not 'feel nothing'. Shankara and Sridhara mean not being swept away by joy or grief, not numbness.
cautions: Sridhara applies the verse directly to the pain of losing loved ones. If it is reused in a grief context, that reading can sound like it reduces bereavement to a passing sensation.
speaks_to: a stressful stretch that will pass
physical or emotional discomfort you can't change right now
not_for: someone in an abusive or unsafe situation
chronic pain or illness that will not 'pass', where 'it comes and goes' can feel invalidating

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.20 (same in all editions checked). Ramanuja's translator notes the parallel verse in Katha Upanishad 1.2.18.
translation_note: Faithful. The phrase 'nāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ' is construed differently by the commentators: Shankara reads 'having been, it does not again cease to be', Sridhara 'it does not come into being again by being born'. Our rendering follows Shankara.
context: Krishna has just said that whoever thinks the self kills, or is killed, does not understand (2.19). This verse gives the reason. The next verse asks how one who knows this could kill or cause killing (2.21). The passage is part of Krishna's answer to Arjuna's horror at killing his kin in battle.

key_terms.sense: it is never born and never dies
unborn, eternal, constant, ancient (Ramanuja: 'old yet ever new')
it is not slain when the body is slain

core_teaching: The self is free of every change that bodies go through, including birth, growth, decay and death. Whatever happens to the body, the self is not destroyed.

commentaries.gist: The verse denies all six changes every being undergoes, from birth to death. The Self has no parts and no qualities to lose, and 'not slain' means it is not altered when the body is.
Birth and death belong to bodies, not to the self. 'Ancient' here means old yet always new, something that can be experienced ever freshly. Bodies perish; the self cannot.
The Self is free of the six transformations from birth to death. Being indivisible, it neither grows nor declines. Birth and death touch only the physical body, never the all-pervading Self.

practical_reading: The verse offers the thought that what a person most deeply is was not ended by the death of their body. Many readers find that a comfort to hold, not an argument to accept.
misreadings: Not a reason to skip mourning or to treat a death as unimportant (as our misuse note says).

Not, in context, a general statement about loss. It is part of Krishna's argument that Arjuna can fight without the self being harmed. The writer should not carry that 'so killing doesn't matter' logic into a grief reading.
cautions: Used on Day 1 of the grief plan ('see'). The surrounding verses (2.11, 2.25, 2.27) draw the conclusion 'therefore you should not grieve'. On a day meant to name the feeling, that conclusion can land as a dismissal. The writer should validate the grief first.
Mentions death and slaying directly.
This passage teaches rebirth. To a newly bereaved reader, a doctrine that the dead simply move on can feel like it skips over their loss.
speaks_to: wanting to believe something of a loved one continues
a sense that a person was more than their body
not_for: someone in the first days of a loss who needs space to mourn, unless the reading leads with acknowledgement
grief after violent death, where the battle context can be jarring
research_note: Sridhara also lists and denies the six changes of being (after Yaska), in agreement with Shankara.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.22 (same in all editions checked).
context: This continues Krishna's argument (2.19–25) that the self is never killed and so Arjuna's grief is misplaced. Just before, he asks how one who knows the self as indestructible could kill or be killed (2.21). Just after, he says weapons, fire, water and wind cannot touch it (2.23).

key_terms.sense: worn-out clothes
takes up (puts on) new ones
casting off worn-out bodies
the embodied self goes on into (others)

core_teaching: Death is like changing clothes. The self lets go of a worn-out body and takes on a new one, and the self itself is not changed by this.

commentaries.gist: Like a person changing old clothes for new, the embodied Self leaves old bodies and enters new ones without itself undergoing any change.
Ramanuja cites scripture: those who fall in a righteous war gain far better bodies. He calls this a cause for rejoicing, like exchanging worn clothes for finer ones.
To someone mourning the body's destruction, Sridhara replies that a new body, shaped by one's actions, will surely follow. Mourning a worn-out body therefore makes no sense.

practical_reading: For those who hold the Gita's view, the image can soften the finality of death: the person has set down a body, not ceased to be. It works as a picture to rest in, not a reason to stop missing someone.
misreadings: Not a line for brushing off someone else's grief (our misuse note is right).
Not a claim that the dead are better off, or that the death was good, even though one classical reading (Ramanuja, about warriors) goes that way.
cautions: This is a strong caution. Used on Day 2 of the grief plan, but both Ramanuja and Sridhara read the verse as removing grounds for grief. Ramanuja even says a warrior's death is matter for rejoicing. The writer must not carry over 'no need to grieve'.
'Worn-out' fits old age. For the death of a child, a young person or a sudden death, the image can feel wrong or hurtful.
This passage teaches rebirth. To a newly bereaved reader, a doctrine that the dead simply move on can feel like it skips over their loss.
speaks_to: wanting a gentle picture of death as transition
a reader whose own tradition holds rebirth
anticipatory grief for an elderly loved one
not_for: loss of a child or a young person
sudden or violent death
early, raw grief

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.23 (same in all editions checked).
context: This is part of Krishna's run of reasons (2.19–25) why the self is never destroyed. It follows the clothes image (2.22). The next two verses call the self uncuttable, eternal and beyond thought, and conclude that knowing this, Arjuna should not grieve (2.25).

key_terms.sense: weapons do not cut it
fire does not burn it
water does not wet (dissolve) it
wind does not dry it

core_teaching: Nothing in the physical world, whether weapon, fire, water or wind, can damage the self, because it is not a physical thing made of parts.

commentaries.gist: The Self has no parts. Weapons cannot divide it, fire cannot reduce it to ash, water cannot loosen it by wetting, and wind cannot dry what has no moisture.

Commenting at 2.24, Ramanuja says the self pervades everything and is subtler than any substance. Cutting, burning, soaking and drying all need to penetrate their object, and nothing can penetrate the self.
The verse spells out the earlier question, 'how can it be slain?', by showing that no means of destruction exists. Water cannot even soften it.
The Self is indivisible, without parts, extremely subtle and infinite, so sword, fire, water and wind have no hold on it.

practical_reading: For a grieving reader it offers one image of steadiness: whatever happened to the body, the self was beyond its reach. It can be held quietly, without arguing anyone out of their sorrow.
misreadings: Not a statement that the body's suffering didn't matter.
Not 'nothing can hurt you' in an everyday sense. It is about the self, not the person's feelings or circumstances.
cautions: Used on Day 4 of the grief plan. The argument it belongs to ends at 2.25 with 'knowing this, you should not grieve', and Ramanuja repeats it. Writers should keep that conclusion out of the reading.
The list of weapons and fire may be painful after a violent death, an accident or a cremation.
speaks_to: needing an image of something in a loved one that was untouched by what happened
finding steadiness on a hard day of grief
not_for: grief after violent death or fire, where the images may be too literal

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.38 (same in all editions checked).
translation_note: Faithful. Note that 'engage in the fight' (yuddhāya yujyasva) literally means 'get ready for battle'. Our line generalises it to 'step in and act', which is a fair application but not what the verse says.
context: Krishna has just argued from worldly honour: a warrior who flees a righteous war loses duty and fame and earns disgrace (2.31–37). This verse closes that argument. With 2.39 he moves from the knowledge of the self to the yoga of action.

key_terms.sense: making pleasure and pain equal, treating them alike
gain and loss, victory and defeat
gird yourself for battle
acting this way you will not incur sin

core_teaching: Act from duty with an even mind towards pleasure and pain, gain and loss, win and defeat. Action done in that spirit does not bind or stain the one who acts.

commentaries.gist: 'Treating alike' means not liking one outcome and disliking the other. Shankara adds that the command to fight is only incidental. The worldly arguments of 2.31–38 just remove grief; the real subject is knowledge of the Self.

Knowing the self as distinct from the body, keep the mind unshaken by pain, gain, loss, victory or defeat. Seek no reward such as heaven and fight as a duty. The 'sin' avoided is the bondage of worldly existence.
This answers Arjuna's fear that sin would overtake him (1.36). Equanimity comes from freedom from elation and despondency. Fighting from duty, without desire for pleasure, incurs no sin.
This is the yoga of equanimity, poise in action. Work done with a balanced mind purifies the heart instead of binding. Such balance is built through continuous struggle and vigilance.

practical_reading: Before a feared task, settle that you will meet a win or a loss with the same steadiness, then commit fully. The fear of the outcome loses some of its grip once the outcome is no longer what defines you.
misreadings: Not 'outcomes don't matter'. It means not being ruled by liking one and dreading the other.
Not a licence to harm others because you feel detached. 'No sin' is tied to doing a rightful duty, not to the attitude alone.
cautions: The verse is literally an order to go into battle against kin. Keep the generalisation to 'act' explicit.
Sridhara links it to Arjuna's fear of sin. Readers with scrupulosity or guilt may need the 'no sin' promise framed carefully.
speaks_to: fear of failing at something important
dreading a result you can't control
needing to commit to a hard task
not_for: someone being pushed into a fight or conflict that is actually wrong

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.40 (same in all editions checked).
translation_note: Faithful. 'This practice' (asya dharmasya) refers specifically to karma-yoga, action without desire for its fruit. The 'great fear' is the fear of saṃsāra, the round of birth and death, in all four commentaries read.
context: Krishna has just announced that he will now teach the yoga of action, by which Arjuna can break the bondage of karma (2.39). This verse is his first promise about it. The next verse contrasts the single resolute mind of this path with the scattered minds of the desire-driven.

key_terms.sense: here no effort begun is lost
no adverse result (harm, reverse effect) arises
even a little of this discipline
protects from the great fear (of birth and death)

core_teaching: Unlike ordinary ventures, an effort on the path of desireless action is never wasted and cannot backfire. Even a small beginning protects you from the great fear of endless rebirth.

commentaries.gist: Unlike farming, nothing attempted on this path is wholly lost. Unlike medicine, it cannot cause harm. However little you do, it saves you from the great fear of saṃsāra, of birth and death.
Even if a duty begun this way is interrupted and left unfinished, no fruit is lost and no harm follows. Ordinary worldly and ritual efforts fail when interrupted and can backfire.

Worldly work and desire-driven rites can fail or backfire through defects. In action done for the Lord, defects do not count, so nothing begun is wasted, and even a start frees one from transmigration.
Each act of karma-yoga purifies the heart at once, so there is no uncertainty, as there is in farming, and no risk, as with a wrong medicine. Krishna praises it to build Arjuna's interest.

practical_reading: Small, sincere steps on an inner practice count, even if you are interrupted or fall short. Starting is itself protective, so you don't have to do it perfectly or completely for it to matter.
misreadings: Not 'no effort is ever wasted' in worldly terms. Shankara and Sivananda explicitly contrast it with farming and medicine, where effort can fail. It does not promise that an exam, launch or project will succeed.
The 'great fear' is the fear of rebirth and bondage, not everyday anxiety, though teachers extend it.
cautions: Used on Day 3 of 'fear of failure'. The writer must not turn it into a promise that worldly effort always pays off. The commentators say the opposite about worldly effort.
speaks_to: fear that starting something will be wasted
feeling that half-done efforts don't count
not_for: someone who needs to hear that a real-world failure was not their fault, if framed as 'effort is never lost'

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.41 (same in all editions checked).
translation_note: Faithful. The line's 'decided mind' versus 'undecided mind' modernises it. In the commentaries the contrast is between a mind set on one aim (liberation, or the Lord) and minds scattered among endless desires. It is not about indecision as such.
context: Following the promise that nothing on this path is wasted (2.40), Krishna contrasts its single resolve with minds driven by many desires. The next verses (2.42–44) criticise people who love the flowery Vedic promises of heaven and power and so never reach a settled mind.

key_terms.sense: resolute, decisive understanding; a settled conviction
single, one-pointed
many-branched … endless
of the irresolute, those without settled conviction

core_teaching: On this path the understanding has one settled aim. People driven by many desires have thoughts that branch without end, and that scatter keeps them bound.

commentaries.gist: On the path to liberation there is one resolute thought, born of right knowledge, which overturns all opposing ones. Following many-branched thoughts makes worldly life endless; when they cease, it ceases too.
The seeker of liberation has a single settled conviction about the self, so all their work points to one aim. Those after rewards like heaven have minds that branch endlessly.
In work done as worship there is one settled conviction: that devotion to the Lord will surely save him. The desire-driven have endless thoughts because their desires are endless.

The yogi gathers the mind's scattered rays through discrimination, dispassion and concentration and stops wavering. The worldly mind breeds countless thoughts; control the thoughts and the mind is controlled.

practical_reading: When a choice feels impossible, ask what your one real aim is. Many options branch out of many wants, and naming the aim prunes them.
misreadings: Not 'be decisive and pick fast'. The resolve comes from clarity about one's highest aim, not from speed.
Not a criticism of considering options carefully. Its target is minds pulled by countless desires.
cautions: In context (2.42–44) the 'irresolute' are those attached to ritual rewards and pleasures. The writer should not imply that an anxious decision-maker is shallow or worldly.
speaks_to: going round in circles on a decision
needing to find the one thing that matters
not_for: someone whose indecision comes from real constraints or danger, not scattered wants

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.47 (same in all editions checked).
context: Krishna has criticised people who perform rituals to gain heaven and power (2.42–46). Now he tells Arjuna how to act instead. The next verse defines yoga as evenness in success and failure (2.48), and 2.49–50 call those who work for the fruit 'pitiable'.

key_terms.sense: your right / claim is to the action alone
never to its fruits
do not let the fruit of action be your motive (or: do not be the cause of the fruit)
and let there be no attachment to not acting

core_teaching: Do the work that is yours and drop the craving for its results. But don't use that as a reason to stop acting: inaction is not the answer either.

commentaries.gist: You are fit for works, not yet for the path of pure knowledge. While working, never thirst for results, since that thirst binds you to rebirth. Nor cling to inaction, asking what use painful works are without their fruits.

For a seeker of liberation, only the doing is yours. Craving and enjoying fruit bind; work done as worship of the Lord, without motive, leads to freedom. Have no interest in Arjuna's 'I will not fight' either.

Answering 'why work if worship brings every result?': you have a right only to action. Do not hanker after results, which bind; undesired results do not arise. But fear of binding work should not push you into inaction.

resentment when something wanted is withheld

An angry man loses discrimination between right and wrong, says and does whatever he likes, and is swept along by impulse into irrational action.

not_for: a reader in a situation of ongoing harm, if the reading implies their anger is the main danger

holding the world together; its welfare, guidance, protection
you ought to act

core_teaching: Wise people like Janaka reached fulfilment while still acting in the world. Even if you needed nothing for yourself, the world's welfare would be reason enough to act.

commentaries.gist: If Janaka and Asvapati had knowledge, they kept acting to set an example. If not, action purified their minds. Either way, Arjuna, born a warrior, should act to protect and guide people.
Royal sages like Janaka, though leaders of the wise, reached self-realisation by works alone. So karma-yoga is commended even to those qualified for the path of knowledge.
Sridhara cites approved precedent: Janaka and others were purified in mind by action and so reached perfection. Even just to give people an incentive, you should act.
Perfection here means liberation. Janaka and others had full self-knowledge, yet kept acting to set an example and guide people.

practical_reading: When nothing feels meaningful for yourself, acting for others can still make sense: a small task done for someone else, or keeping a commitment others rely on.
misreadings: Not 'your worth is your usefulness'. The verse offers a reason to act, not a measure of a person.
Not 'ignore your own emptiness and keep busy'.
cautions: Used on Day 6 of 'nothing matters'. If the reader may be depressed, 'keep working for the world' should be offered gently, with a small, concrete act, not as an obligation.
not_for: someone in a depressive crisis who needs care, not duty

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.21 (same in all editions checked).
context: Krishna has just told Arjuna to act for the world's welfare (3.20). This verse explains why: people imitate their leaders. He goes on to say that he himself, who needs nothing, keeps acting, because if he stopped, people would follow and the world would fall into ruin (3.22–24).

key_terms.sense: whatever the best / most respected person does
that very thing other people do
sets up as the standard / authority
the world follows it

core_teaching: People take their cue from those they look up to. So anyone with standing is responsible for the standard their conduct sets.

commentaries.gist: Whatever authority a leading person follows, in spiritual or worldly matters, his followers take as their authority too.
People who know what ought to be done still wait for a respected person to lead. So he must set the example through his duties. Failing is a wrong against the world and harms his own progress.
The masses copy a great person, and whichever scripture he treats as authoritative, whether it teaches action or renunciation, people follow.
Humans are social and imitative. They take their sense of right and wrong from those they regard as morally superior and try to walk in their footsteps.

practical_reading: With success comes influence. People around you, especially juniors, family or followers, will copy how you work, treat others and handle pressure, so set the standard you want them to follow.
misreadings: Not 'successful people are better people'. The verse is about responsibility, not superiority.
Not 'image management'. The point is real conduct, not appearances.
cautions: Ramanuja frames the leader's duty in terms of the duties of his caste (varṇa) and stage of life. Don't import that framing.
speaks_to: being a parent or role model
not_for: someone already crushed by others' expectations, if framed as 'everyone is watching you'

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.30 (same in all editions checked).
translation_note: Faithful. Note: 'me' (mayi) is Krishna himself. Our line's 'something higher' is a softened generalisation. The commentators unanimously read jvara ('fever') as grief or anguish.
context: Krishna has explained that actions are really done by the forces of nature, though the ego thinks 'I am the doer' (3.27–29). Here he tells Arjuna how to act: offer every action to him, keep the mind on the self, and fight without hope, possessiveness or fever. The next verses promise freedom to those who follow this teaching with faith (3.31–32).

key_terms.sense: resigning / offering all actions to me
with the mind turned to the self (inner reality)
free from hope (expectation) and from 'mine'
fight, with your fever (anguish, grief) gone

core_teaching: Offer all your actions to the Lord, keep your mind on the inner self, drop expectation and possessiveness, and do your work free of anguish.

commentaries.gist: Surrender all actions to Vasudeva, the Self of all, with the thought: 'I, the agent, do this for the Lord's sake, as his servant.' 'Fever' means anguish or grief.

Place all acts in Krishna, the inner Self of all beings, contemplating the self as his body, ruled from within. Desireless and free of 'mine' and cankering care, 'fight' here means discharge all prescribed duties.
You have not yet realised the truth, so act. Offer each action to the Lord, knowing the Inner Ruler guides you. Drop expectation and any sense that the action is for your own ends, and banish grief.
Surrender all actions with the thought 'I do everything for the Lord's sake'. Fever here means grief or sorrow.

practical_reading: Before a stressful task, consciously hand it over, as an offering or simply as 'not mine to control'. Then do it without the anxious grip. The fever (the heat of worry and grief) can drop while the work still gets done.
misreadings: Not handing over your judgement or responsibility (our misuse note is right). The commentators still expect full, careful action.
Not literally a call to fight, except in Arjuna's setting. Ramanuja reads 'fight' as 'do your prescribed duties'.
cautions: The 'me' is Krishna. For a general audience, 'something higher' is acceptable, but don't misrepresent the verse as non-theistic.
speaks_to: needing to let go of control
not_for: someone whose stress comes from being pressured to do something wrong

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.35 (same in all editions checked). The first half recurs almost word for word at 18.47.
translation_note: The translation is faithful. Editor flag: our misuse note ('not the role your birth assigned; your own nature and calling') states a modern reading as if it were the verse's meaning. The classical readings differ. Shankara, Sridhara and Sivananda take svadharma as the duty of one's station (for Arjuna, a warrior's duty to fight), and Sridhara and Shankara say another's duty leads to hell. Ramanuja reads it as the path that suits you, karma-yoga, against the harder path of knowledge. Present 'own nature and calling' as a modern application, and say the classical frame is station-based.
context: Krishna has warned that everyone acts according to their nature and that attraction and aversion lie in wait in every sense-object (3.33–34). This verse concludes the section. It also prompts Arjuna's next question: what makes a person do wrong even against their will (3.36)?

key_terms.sense: one's own duty / proper way of life
imperfect, lacking merit
than another's duty, even well performed
another's duty brings fear / danger

core_teaching: Doing your own proper duty imperfectly is better than doing someone else's well. Even death in your own duty is better, because another's path brings danger.

commentaries.gist: Dying while doing your own duty, however imperfect, beats living by another's duty done flawlessly, since another's duty brings peril, hell among them.

Here 'own dharma' means karma-yoga, which comes naturally and safely to someone bound to matter. The path of knowledge is excellent but hard and risky for them. Even if death comes first, progress carries over to the next birth.

Someone might prefer another's easier duty, like non-violence, to his own harsh one, like war. Sridhara rejects this: one's own flawed duty still ranks higher. Dying in it brings heaven; another's forbidden duty brings hell.
A warrior's duty is to fight a righteous battle. Arjuna should fight, even at the cost of his life, and not abandon his duty for the path of renunciation, which belongs to others.

practical_reading: Modern teachers apply it against comparison: a life lived honestly on your own terms, even clumsily, beats a polished imitation of someone else's. (This is an application. The classical commentators tie svadharma to one's station or one's suited path.)
misreadings: Do not present 'your own calling' as what the verse plainly means. That is a modern reading.
Not an endorsement of caste or birth-assigned roles. The app should not carry the classical station-based reading forward uncritically either.
Not 'never try something new'. It warns against abandoning your own path out of imitation or fear.
cautions: Mentions death ('better is death in one's own duty'). Handle carefully with a distressed reader.
Caste: three of the four commentaries read it in terms of varṇa or station, and Shankara and Sridhara mention hell. The editor should decide how the app frames this.
speaks_to: feeling pressure to live someone else's life
not_for: someone being told to stay in a role imposed by family, caste or gender
a reader with suicidal thoughts (the 'death' line)

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.36 (same in all editions checked).
attribution_note: Arjuna to Krishna is right (the Sanskrit includes 'arjuna uvāca'). Minor data glitch: the Sanskrit field runs 'अर्जुन उवाचअथ' together without a space.
context: Krishna has just said that attraction and aversion lie in wait in the senses and should not be allowed to rule, and that one's own duty is better than another's (3.34–35). Arjuna asks what drives people into wrongdoing even against their will. Krishna's answer names desire, which becomes anger, as the enemy (3.37–43).

key_terms.sense: driven / impelled by what (is this person)
does a person commit wrong (sin)
even though unwilling
as if compelled by force

core_teaching: Arjuna asks the question everyone asks: why do I do the wrong thing when part of me doesn't want to, as if something forces me?

commentaries.gist: Shankara pictures a person dragged and constrained the way a king's servant is pushed into tasks. Krishna answers that he will name the enemy who is the source of all evil.
Arjuna asks what impels a person who wants to pursue the path of knowledge, dragging him as if by force into evil ways.
Arjuna doubts anyone can avoid coming under desire's sway. Even people who restrain desire and anger through discernment are seen slipping back, so he suspects a deeper prompter at the root of both.

practical_reading: Naming the pattern ('I keep doing this even though I don't want to') is the first honest step. The Gita treats it as a real question deserving a real answer, not as proof that you are bad.
misreadings: Not an excuse ('something forced me'). The answer that follows locates the force in one's own desire, which can be mastered.
Not a verdict that the asker is wicked. It is a sincere question from the Gita's hero.
cautions: Used on Day 1 of the guilt plan. Krishna's answer calls desire the 'enemy' and 'greatly sinful' (3.37). For a reader with heavy guilt or shame, keep the focus on understanding, not condemnation.
If the reader's 'wrong thing' is an addiction, the verse speaks to it, but the plan should not imply that willpower alone is the fix.
not_for: a reader who has been harmed and is blaming themselves for another person's wrongdoing
research_note: Sivananda only glosses the name 'Varshneya' here, so he is not listed.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.37 (same in all editions checked).
attribution_note: Krishna to Arjuna is right. Minor data glitch: the Sanskrit field runs 'श्री भगवानुवाचकाम' together without a space.
translation_note: Faithful. mahāśanaḥ is literally 'of huge appetite' (Sridhara: it cannot be appeased by giving it what it wants). mahāpāpmā is 'greatly sinful'; 'greatly harmful' softens it slightly, which is fine for the app.
context: Krishna answers Arjuna's question (3.36): the force that drives people to wrongdoing is desire, which becomes anger when blocked. He goes on to say it covers wisdom like smoke covers fire or dust a mirror (3.38–39), and that one must master the senses to slay it (3.41–43).

key_terms.sense: it is desire, it is anger (one force in two forms)
born of rajas, the quality of restless passion
all-devouring, of insatiable appetite
greatly sinful … the enemy

core_teaching: Desire, and anger as its blocked form, both born of restless passion, can never be satisfied. That is the real enemy behind wrongdoing.

commentaries.gist: Desire is the whole world's enemy and the source of all evil. When obstructed, it becomes wrath, so wrath is desire itself. Rousing rajas, it drives people to act; we hear them say 'desire made me do it'.
Craving for sense-objects, sharpened by past habit, is a devouring foe. Blocked, it turns into hatred towards whoever stands in the way, even leading to violence. It obstructs the path of knowledge.
Anger is desire frustrated, so conquering desire conquers anger. It arises from rajas and fades as sattva (clarity) grows. It cannot be appeased by feeding it; it must be overcome.
Desire is the root of wrong action. Anger is desire unfulfilled, turned against whatever obstructs it. Born of rajas, desire stirs a person into restless striving to possess.

practical_reading: Behind a flash of anger there is usually a want or expectation that got blocked. Tracing anger back to the desire underneath gives you something you can actually work with.
misreadings: Not 'all desire is evil'. The commentators target craving, the insatiable kind driven by rajas.
Not 'you are your anger'. It is called an enemy precisely because it is not the self.
cautions: Strong words ('greatly sinful', 'enemy'). For a reader ashamed of anger, frame desire as something that can be understood and mastered, not a mark of badness.
speaks_to: frustration when things don't go your way
not_for: anger at injustice or abuse, if framed as 'your desire is the problem'

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.17 (same in all editions checked).
attribution_note: Speaker and listener are right, but the setting is wrong for this verse. 'Krishna reveals the ancient lineage of this teaching and why he comes into the world' describes 4.1–8. Verse 4.17 sits in 4.16–18, where Krishna says even the wise are confused about what action and inaction are, and promises to explain. Suggest: 'Krishna to Arjuna: even sages are confused about what counts as action, wrong action and inaction.'
translation_note: Acceptable. Readings of vikarma differ. Shankara and Sridhara take it as unlawful or prohibited action. Ramanuja takes it as the variety of everyday and desire-driven acts (including earning money), and akarma as knowledge. The line's 'when to hold back' for akarma is a modern gloss. In the commentaries akarma is the true nature of non-action, explained in 4.18 (seeing inaction in action).
context: Krishna has said that even sages are bewildered about what action and inaction are, and promised to explain the action that frees (4.16). This verse says all three need understanding. The next verse gives the famous paradox: the wise see inaction in action and action in inaction (4.18).

key_terms.sense: (the nature) of action must be understood
of wrong / prohibited action (Ramanuja: the many kinds of action)
of inaction, non-action
deep / hard to fathom is the way of action

core_teaching: What counts as right action, wrong action and non-action is not obvious. It has to be understood carefully, because the way of action is deep.

commentaries.gist: There is much to learn about action enjoined by scripture, about unlawful action, and about inaction. The true nature of all three is hard to grasp, and Krishna goes on to explain it.

Three things must be known: action that leads to liberation; the many actions (daily, occasional, desire-driven) and the earning they require; and akarma, which here means knowledge. So the path of action is abstruse.
People assume action is bodily movement and inaction its absence. But the true nature of enjoined action, of forbidden action and of non-action must each be learned. Their way is mysterious.

practical_reading: Before a hard decision, slow down and look at what you are actually doing, what would be wrong, and what not acting would really mean. Rarely is any of the three as obvious as it first seems.
misreadings: Not 'everything is relative'. The verse says right and wrong action must be understood, not that they don't exist.
Not 'doing nothing is always an option'. The next verse shows that inaction can itself be a form of action.
speaks_to: not knowing whether to act or wait
not_for: someone who needs a clear, immediate safety decision rather than reflection
research_note: Sivananda gives only a translation for this verse.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.22 (same in all editions checked).
context: Krishna is describing the wise who act without being bound (4.18–23). Before this, he says that one who has given up attachment to results, ever content and dependent on nothing, does nothing even while acting (4.20–21). After it, he says that for one whose work is done as sacrifice, all action dissolves (4.23).

key_terms.sense: content with whatever comes of its own accord, unsought
gone beyond the pairs of opposites (heat and cold, pleasure and pain)
free from envy / malice
even acting, he is not bound

core_teaching: The person who is content with what comes, steady through life's opposites, free of envy and even in success and failure, can act without being bound by the action.

commentaries.gist: He is content with what comes unasked, unshaken by opposites and free of envy. Whether he gets his bodily needs or not, he stays calm, knowing the Self is not the doer, so in truth he does nothing.

He takes what comes for his upkeep and patiently bears opposites. He is free of malice because he traces harm that befalls him to his own past deeds, not to others. Balanced in success or failure, he is not fettered.
Content with whatever arrives unsought, enduring opposites, without jealousy, and unmoved whether luck brings something or nothing, he stays unbound even while performing actions.

The sage is satisfied with whatever comes by chance and stays balanced. Others see him acting, but he knows the qualities of Nature do everything. His actions are burnt in knowledge like roasted seeds.

practical_reading: Comparison lives on envy and on keeping score of others' gains. Practising contentment with what has come to you, and evenness about wins and losses, loosens its grip while you keep working.
misreadings: Not 'never want anything better'. It is about contentment and freedom from envy, not giving up effort.
Not 'blame yourself for everything'. Ramanuja's gloss (tracing harm to one's own past karma) is a doctrinal point, not advice to take on blame for others' wrongs.
cautions: Ramanuja's reading of 'free of malice' (attribute harm to your own past deeds, not to others) could be heard by a mistreated reader as 'it's your fault'. Avoid it in that context.
not_for: someone who has been wronged and needs to name it

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.34 (same in all editions checked).
context: This is part of Krishna's praise of knowledge (4.33–42), which ends chapter 4. Krishna has just said that the sacrifice of knowledge is higher than any material offering, and that all action culminates in knowledge (4.33). This verse says how to get it: from those who have seen the truth. The following verses describe what that knowledge does: it ends delusion and carries even the worst wrongdoer across (4.35–36).

key_terms.sense: by humble prostration, reverence
by thorough questioning
by service
the wise who have seen the truth

core_teaching: Learn the deepest knowledge from people who have actually realised it. Approach them with humility, ask real questions and serve.

commentaries.gist: Go to teachers, prostrate humbly, and ask: what is bondage, what is liberation, what is knowledge, what is ignorance? Serve them. Only knowledge passed on by those who have realised the truth, not merely learned it, is effective.

Learn the self-knowledge taught in 2.17–39 from the wise, step by step as you carry on your work, through reverence, timely questions and service. Pleased, they will discern what you truly want to know and teach it.

Prostrate fully before realised people, ask them where your worldly existence comes from and how it can end, and attend on them. Those learned in scripture and with direct experience will instruct you.

Seek a teacher both learned in scripture and established in Brahman; book learning alone is not enough. Prostration alone can be hypocrisy. What counts is faith, sincere questions and wholehearted service.

practical_reading: In your first week with the Gita: find a trustworthy teacher, study circle or commentary, come with humility, ask your real questions, and give something back. Learning deepens in relationship, not just reading.
misreadings: Not 'obey a guru unquestioningly'. paripraśna means probing questions, and the commentators insist the teacher must have truly realised what they teach.
Not 'service' in the sense of unpaid labour or submission to anyone claiming authority.
cautions: Guru-devotion language (prostration, service, perfect faith) has been exploited by abusive teachers. The writer should stress discernment in choosing a teacher.
speaks_to: having questions you're afraid to ask
not_for: someone leaving or recovering from a high-control religious group

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.36 (same in all editions checked).
context: This is part of Krishna's praise of knowledge (4.33–42), which ends chapter 4. Krishna has said that with this knowledge Arjuna will never again fall into such delusion and will see all beings in himself and in Krishna (4.35). This verse makes the strongest claim, and the next gives the fire image (4.37).

key_terms.sense: even if you are the worst of all wrongdoers
by the raft / boat of knowledge
you will cross over all wrongdoing (crookedness, sin)

core_teaching: No one is beyond redemption. Even the worst wrongdoer can cross the whole ocean of their wrongdoing on the boat of true knowledge.

commentaries.gist: Knowledge is a boat for crossing the whole sea of wrongdoing. To a seeker of liberation, Shankara adds, even merit is something to be left behind.
Even if you were a greater sinner than the greatest, the bark of self-knowledge would carry you across the sea of long-hoarded sins.
Even someone foremost among wrongdoers will cross the entire sea of wrongdoing easily, with knowledge as the only vessel needed.
The boat of self-knowledge carries one across the ocean of sin. Sivananda points to 9.30 for the same assurance.

practical_reading: Guilt can make a person feel permanently defined by what they did. The verse insists that real understanding can carry anyone across: the past does not get the final word.
misreadings: Not 'understanding cancels the harm done to others' (our misuse note is right). It is about inner liberation, not erasing consequences or skipping amends.
Not a licence ('I can do wrong now and get knowledge later').
cautions: Used on Day 2 of the guilt plan. 'Most sinful of all sinners' can sting a reader already full of shame. Emphasise the promise, not the label.
speaks_to: wanting to start again after wrongdoing
not_for: someone avoiding responsibility for ongoing harm to others

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.37 (same in all editions checked).
context: This is part of Krishna's praise of knowledge (4.33–42), which ends chapter 4. After promising that knowledge carries even the worst wrongdoer across (4.36), Krishna gives a stronger image: knowledge does not just cross over past actions, it burns them up. The next verse says there is no purifier equal to knowledge (4.38).

key_terms.sense: as a kindled fire (burns) firewood
reduces to ashes
the fire of knowledge (burns) all actions (their karmic residue)

core_teaching: Real knowledge of the self works like fire on fuel. It takes away the power of past actions to keep binding a person.

commentaries.gist: Knowledge cannot literally burn actions. It makes them impotent. Actions whose effects have already begun, which produced this body, run their course; knowledge destroys only those not yet bearing fruit.
As a kindled fire burns a bundle of sticks, knowledge of the self's true nature reduces to ashes the whole long-accumulated mass of sin clinging to the individual soul.
This verse prevents a misreading of the last one: sin is not just crossed while it remains, like an ocean, but destroyed. All actions burn, except prārabdha.

Like roasted seeds, actions burnt by knowledge cannot sprout or bind a person to rebirth. Without the sense 'I do this' and without desire for fruit, action loses its potency. Prārabdha is the usual exception.

practical_reading: Understanding can change your relationship to the past: old actions stop dictating who you are. Making amends and living with consequences still belong to the same honest process.
misreadings: Not 'no consequences'. Shankara, Sridhara and Sivananda all say knowledge does not burn up prārabdha karma, the past action whose effects have already begun (it produced this body). Those effects still play out.
Not a way to skip accountability (our misuse note is right).
cautions: Used on Day 3 of the guilt plan. The prārabdha point supports the plan's message that amends still matter, and the writer can use it.
speaks_to: feeling defined by what you did
not_for: someone looking for absolution while still harming others

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.42 (same in all editions checked). It is the last verse of chapter 4.
translation_note: Faithful, but it omits ātmanaḥ. Shankara insists this means the doubt 'concerning the Self', and Sivananda renders 'the doubt of the self'. Consider 'this doubt about the self, born of ignorance'. 'Take refuge in yoga' (yogam ātiṣṭha) means 'resort to / establish yourself in yoga' (karma-yoga, per all four commentators).
context: This ends chapter 4. Krishna has just said that the doubter perishes and finds no happiness in this world or the next, while one who has given up action through yoga and cut doubt by knowledge is not bound (4.40–41). Here he tells Arjuna to cut his doubt, take up yoga and stand up. Chapter 5 opens with Arjuna, still uncertain, asking which is better: renunciation or action.

key_terms.sense: born of ignorance, lodged in the heart
cutting it with the sword of knowledge
the doubt (about the self)
resort to yoga, and stand up!

core_teaching: Cut through the doubt that ignorance has planted in your heart with clear understanding. Then commit to the path of action and stand up.

commentaries.gist: Doubt is most sinful, born of ignorance and lodged in the intellect. Kill it with right knowledge of the Self, which removes grief and folly. Then take up karma-yoga and arise to fight.
With the knowledge of the self that Krishna has taught, sever your long-standing doubts about the self. Practise karma-yoga as instructed, and arise to carry out his teaching.

Cut the doubt arising from grief, born of not knowing the Self, with the sword of discrimination between Self and body. Take up karma-yoga and first of all rise for the battle at hand, which is righteous for a warrior.
Doubt torments the mind. It is born of ignorance. Cut it down with self-knowledge, then stand up and act.

practical_reading: At a new start, some doubt is natural. But when it becomes a loop that keeps you from moving, use what you know to cut it, choose your path and take the first step today.
misreadings: Not 'never question anything'. The doubt meant here is confusion about the self that paralyses action, not honest inquiry (4.34 praises questioning).
Not literally 'go to war', except in Arjuna's case.
cautions: Shankara and Sivananda call doubt 'most sinful'. For an anxious or OCD-prone reader, that can feed self-blame. Frame it as 'doubt that stops you', not 'doubting is a sin'.
not_for: someone whose doubt is a healthy warning about a harmful choice

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.10 (same in all editions checked).
translation_note: Follows Shankara and Sridhara: brahmaṇi ādhāya means offering actions to the Lord / Supreme. Ramanuja reads brahman here as prakṛti (matter, citing 14.3): one ascribes actions to matter and thinks 'I do nothing'. Both are legitimate. 'The Supreme' is fine for the app.
context: In chapter 5 Krishna is reconciling renunciation and action. He has just said that the one who knows the truth thinks 'I do nothing at all' even while seeing, hearing and eating, since only the senses move among their objects (5.8–9). This verse gives the lotus-leaf image. The next says yogis act with body, mind and intellect only to purify themselves (5.11).

key_terms.sense: placing / offering actions in Brahman (the Lord; for Ramanuja, matter)
giving up attachment
he is not stained by sin
like a lotus leaf by water

core_teaching: Whoever acts while offering the action up and letting go of attachment stays unstained by it, as a lotus leaf sits in water without getting wet.

commentaries.gist: He offers all actions to the Lord, like a servant acting for his master, without attachment even to liberation. The only result of acting this way is a purified mind.

Here 'brahman' means matter. Whoever sees that seeing and hearing belong to matter and the senses, ascribes actions to it, and thinks 'I do nothing' is untouched by the error of taking matter for the self.

Objection: one who feels 'I am the doer' must be tainted, so how can he renounce? Answer: offering actions to the Lord and dropping attachment to fruit, he is untouched by good or evil deeds, like a lotus leaf.

Several verses in chapters 4–5 make one point: the yogi who acts without ego or attachment to results, offering everything to the Lord, is not tainted, gains purity of heart and, through it, self-knowledge.

practical_reading: In a stressful environment you can do your work fully without letting the drama and politics soak in. The 'leaf' is the inner distance that comes from doing the work as an offering, not as a bid for approval.
misreadings: Not 'stay silent about wrongdoing' (our misuse note is right). Being unstained is about inner freedom, not complicity.
Not 'nothing you do can be wrong if you're detached'. The verse is about how a rightful action is done.
speaks_to: feeling contaminated by a toxic environment
wanting to stay clean inside while staying engaged
not_for: someone in an abusive situation who needs to leave, not stay 'unstained'

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.18 (same in all editions checked).
translation_note: Literal, but the editor needs to look at this. śvapāka ('dog-cooker') is a caste slur-term for people treated as outcastes; Sastri's footnote glosses it as 'chandala, an outcaste'. Our line renders it 'an outcast', which reads as endorsing the category. Suggest wording like 'a person society shuns as an outcaste', or use the Sanskrit with a note.

Krishna has just said that knowledge dispels ignorance like the sun (5.16), and that those whose minds are absorbed in it are freed from rebirth (5.17). This verse defines their vision. The next says those whose minds rest in this sameness have conquered worldly existence here and now (5.19).

key_terms.sense: in a brahmin endowed with learning and humility
in a cow, an elephant, a dog
in a 'dog-cooker', a term for those treated as outcastes
the wise are equal-seeing

core_teaching: The wise see the same Self in every being, however different their species, learning or social status.

commentaries.gist: These beings illustrate the widest differences of outward form. The wise see every self as equal, because all share the same essential nature, consciousness. The differences belong to matter, not to the self.
These beings differ in their guṇas, but the sage sees in each the one immutable Self, untouched by those qualities. (Shankara does rank them: brahmin sattvic, cow rajasic, the rest tamasic.)
The wise see one principle, Brahman, in unlike things. The brahmin and the 'dog-cooker' illustrate differences of conduct; the cow, elephant and dog, differences of species.
The liberated sage sees only the Self everywhere. As the sun's reflection is unaffected by a clean river or a dirty stream, the Self is unaffected by the bodies it appears in.

practical_reading: Success tempts us to rank people by status. The verse asks for the opposite practice: treat the person who serves you, the stranger and the colleague with the same regard you give the powerful.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of the caste hierarchy its examples come from. Its point is that those distinctions don't touch the Self.
Not 'treat everyone identically in practice'. Shankara notes it is about seeing the same Self, not about erasing all practical distinctions.
cautions: This is a strong caution about caste. Shankara and Sivananda explicitly rank the beings by guṇa and group the outcaste with animals as tamasic. Shankara's comment goes on to discuss a law about not eating such persons' food. Do not reproduce those rankings. Ramanuja's reading (all selves equal in essence) is the safest to lead with.
Our line's 'an outcast' should be reworded.
speaks_to: treating people fairly regardless of status
not_for: readers who may be hurt by casual use of caste terms

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.21 (same in all editions checked).
context: This is part of Krishna's description of the sage who has realised Brahman (5.18–26), late in chapter 5. Krishna has just described the knower of Brahman as neither elated by the pleasant nor shaken by the unpleasant (5.20). This verse describes their inner joy. The next adds that pleasures born of contact are wombs of sorrow, with a beginning and an end (5.22).

key_terms.sense: one whose mind is unattached to external contacts (sense-pleasures)
finds the happiness that is in the self
with mind joined to Brahman through yoga
enjoys undecaying happiness

core_teaching: When the mind is no longer hooked by outer pleasures, it finds a joy within. Joined to Brahman, that joy does not run out.

commentaries.gist: When the mind is not tied to external sense-objects, the sage finds the joy in the Self. Absorbed in deep contemplation of Brahman, he gains imperishable bliss, so one should turn the senses from momentary pleasures.
Whoever stops clinging to pleasures from things other than the self, and begins to delight in the self within, unites his mind to repeated contemplation of the self and gains imperishable bliss.
Unattached to outer objects, he first finds the serene joy of inner withdrawal. Then, with his mind absorbed in Brahman through yoga, he enjoys a bliss that never decays.
To enjoy the imperishable happiness within, withdraw the senses from their objects and go deep into meditation on the Self.

practical_reading: Notice the difference between pleasure that needs something outside you and the quieter gladness that comes in stillness. Giving the second a few minutes a day helps it grow.
misreadings: Not 'outer joys are bad'. It contrasts dependent pleasure with independent joy.
Not a call to withdraw from relationships.
cautions: The very next verse (5.22) calls sense-pleasures 'wombs of sorrow'. In a joy plan, the writer should not slide into treating all ordinary happiness as suspect.
not_for: someone with anhedonia or depression, if framed as 'joy is simply within, just find it'

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.23 (same in all editions checked).
context: This is part of Krishna's description of the sage who has realised Brahman (5.18–26), late in chapter 5. Krishna has just called sense-pleasures wombs of sorrow with a beginning and an end (5.22). Here he says the truly disciplined and happy person can withstand the surge of desire and anger right here, in this life. The next verse describes the one whose joy and light are within (5.24).

key_terms.sense: who is able, right here, to withstand
before release from the body (i.e. for as long as one lives)
the surge / impulse born of desire and anger
he is disciplined (harmonised); he is a happy person

core_teaching: Whoever can withstand the surge of desire and anger here and now, for as long as they live, is the disciplined one, and truly happy.

commentaries.gist: 'Before release from the body' makes death the limit: desire and anger pull all life long and are never to be trusted. Desire shows as bristling and glee, anger as trembling, sweating, fiery eyes. Withstanding them is happiness.
Even while still practising, in the body, one who draws on the satisfying experience of the self to resist the rush of desire and passion is fit for yoga, and finds bliss in the self.
The surge of desire and anger is the great enemy of liberation. Withstand it the moment it bubbles up, and keep doing so till death, not just for a moment. Only such a person is poised and happy.
Desire and anger are powerful enemies of peace and need strong effort to overcome. The happiest person is the one who has mastered them, not the one with great wealth or a picture-perfect family.

practical_reading: Anger arrives as a surge in the body: heat, trembling, a clenched jaw. You don't have to act on it. Riding out the wave without obeying it is a skill you can practise today.
misreadings: Not 'never feel desire or anger'. It is about withstanding the surge, not having no surge.
'Before leaving the body' is about the whole span of life, not a hint about death.
cautions: Mentions death ('before release from the body'; Shankara: 'up to the point of death'). One of Sridhara's alternative readings compares the steady person to a corpse unmoved by mourners or the funeral pyre. Don't use that gloss with a distressed reader.
not_for: a reader with suicidal thoughts, if the 'before death' phrasing is emphasised

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.24 (same in all editions checked).
translation_note: Follows the Advaita reading ('becomes one with Brahman'). Ramanuja reads brahma-bhūtaḥ as 'Brahman-like' (the self restored to its pure nature), and brahma-nirvāṇa as the bliss of self-experience. A neutral rendering would be 'becomes Brahman-like and reaches the peace of Brahman'.
context: This is part of Krishna's description of the sage who has realised Brahman (5.18–26), late in chapter 5. After the person who withstands desire and anger (5.23), Krishna describes the one whose happiness, delight and light are all within. The following verses say such sages, free of sin and doubt and devoted to all beings' welfare, attain Brahman's peace (5.25–26).

key_terms.sense: whose happiness is within
whose delight (pleasure-garden) is within
whose light is within
the peace / bliss of Brahman … having become Brahman (Ramanuja: Brahman-like)

core_teaching: The yogi whose happiness, delight and light all come from within attains the peace of Brahman, even while living.

commentaries.gist: 'Within' means in the Self. Such a yogi attains liberation, the bliss in Brahman, while still living on earth, himself becoming Brahman.

Having let go of external pleasures, he longs for the joy of self-experience. The self is his pleasure-garden and knowledge of the self his only light. Such a Brahman-like yogi gains the bliss of self-enjoyment.

Subduing desire and anger is not enough. Happiness must rest in the Self, not in objects; one's play must be within, and one's attention inward rather than on entertainments. Only then is one absorbed in Brahman.
Within means in the Self. Such a yogi attains liberation while still living, becoming a jīvanmukta.

practical_reading: Joy that comes from within (from meaning, presence, a quiet mind) is less fragile than joy that depends on events. Notice where your gladness comes from, and tend the inner source.
misreadings: Not 'needing nothing and no one'. It describes where the deepest joy comes from, not a rejection of people.
cautions: Used on Day 1 of the joy plan ('see'). Keep it invitational. A reader without much inner joy right now should not come away feeling deficient.
speaks_to: wanting joy that doesn't depend on circumstances
not_for: someone isolated, if framed as 'you don't need others'

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.29 (same in all editions checked). It is the last verse of chapter 5.
attribution_note: Speaker and listener are right. The setting ('briefly describing meditation') fits 5.27–28. This verse is the closing statement that follows: knowing the Lord as friend of all brings peace.
context: Krishna has just sketched meditation: shut out external contacts, fix the gaze between the brows, even out the breath, and be free of desire, fear and anger (5.27–28). This verse closes chapter 5 with what the meditator should know. Chapter 6 then teaches meditation in detail.

key_terms.sense: the enjoyer / recipient of sacrifices and austerities
the great lord of all the worlds
the friend (well-wisher) of all beings
attains peace

core_teaching: Knowing the Lord as the one who receives every offering, rules all the worlds and is the selfless friend of every being, a person comes to peace.

commentaries.gist: I am Narayana, author and goal of all sacrifices and austerities, everyone's friend, doing good without expecting return. Dwelling in all hearts, I dispense the fruits of action and witness all thought. Knowing me brings peace, saṃsāra's end.
Knowing Krishna as receiver of sacrifices, Lord of lords and intimate friend of every creature, one finds peace. Work done as worship is easiest, and who would not gladly serve a universal friend?

Liberation needs knowledge, not just sense-control. Know the Lord as the one who protects his devotees' offerings, the great Lord, and the disinterested well-wisher or inner ruler of all; by his grace one attains peace.
The Lord is the friend of all beings, doing them good without expecting anything back, dwelling in their hearts as silent witness. Knowing him, they attain peace and liberation.

practical_reading: In loneliness, the verse offers a companion that is always present: the divine as a well-wisher who wants your good and expects nothing in return. Many readers find that thought steadying, alongside human connection.
misreadings: Not 'you don't need human friends'. It offers a deeper companionship, not a replacement.
Not a transactional God. The commentators stress that the Lord does good without expecting return.
cautions: Theistic verse: 'me' is Krishna. Our line's 'the divine' is a reasonable softening, but don't strip the theism entirely.
not_for: a non-theistic reader, unless framed as the Gita's view
someone in crisis who needs human support urgently

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 6.5 (same in all editions checked).
translation_note: Faithful. ātman is used in several senses. Ramanuja reads the instrument ātmanā as 'by the mind': the mind lifts or harms the self. Shankara and Sridhara read the self's own discrimination and effort.
context: Krishna opens chapter 6 by saying the true renouncer is one who does their duty without depending on its fruit (6.1). For one climbing to yoga, action is the means; for one who has arrived, calm is (6.3–4). This verse says the climb is one's own to make. The next explains: the self is a friend to one who has mastered it, and acts like an enemy to one who hasn't (6.6).

key_terms.sense: one should lift oneself by oneself
one should not let oneself sink / degrade oneself
the self alone is the self's friend (kin)
the self alone is the self's enemy

core_teaching: Lift yourself up by your own effort and don't drag yourself down. Depending on how you treat yourself, you are your own best friend or your own worst enemy.

commentaries.gist: Here 'by the self' means by the mind. A mind detached from sense-pleasures lifts the self to higher things; turned towards objects, it harasses the self. So the mind is the self's friend or foe, depending on its use.

Since attachment binds and non-attachment frees, use your discriminating self to lift yourself out of worldly bondage and never degrade yourself. The self freed from attachment is your benefactor; otherwise it is your enemy.

One drowning in worldly existence should lift himself by practising yoga. No one else can liberate you. Shankara even calls outer friends obstacles, as objects of attachment, and says outer enemies are made enemies by oneself.
Discipline the mind and senses and rise. Friends and enemies are really in the mind: the impure mind binds you and is your enemy, and the pure mind helps you to freedom and is your friend.

practical_reading: Notice how you talk to yourself. Treat yourself as you'd treat a friend who's struggling: encourage the next step instead of piling on, because you can be the one who pulls you up.
misreadings: Not 'you're alone, so don't ask for help' (our misuse note is right). Arjuna himself asks for help.
Not 'it's all your fault'. The verse is about agency, not blame.
cautions: This is a strong caution. Shankara and Sivananda say outward friends are obstacles or 'enemies in reality' for a seeker. The verse is used in the losing-hope and comparison plans, and possibly by lonely readers, so the writer must not pass on that view.
For a reader losing hope, 'raise yourself by yourself' can sound like 'you're on your own'. Pair it with permission to seek support.
not_for: someone in crisis who needs to hear that others can and should help them
a lonely reader, if Shankara's or Sivananda's view of friends is carried over
